::: {.why}
The R-squared you found last night is two orders of magnitude above anything in your daily work, and understanding why that does not make it a strategy is the most useful lesson in the week.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Report the predictive R-squared of order flow imbalance for mid returns at several horizons and show the decay.
- Say why a high short-horizon R-squared does not survive the round-trip cost, with the arithmetic.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Map the decay: regress mid change on order flow imbalance at horizons from 100 milliseconds to 10 minutes, and plot R-squared against horizon. It falls off a cliff, and where it crosses your cost threshold is the boundary of the game you are not in.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Do the arithmetic that closes the question: at the R-squared you measured, the expected move over the horizon in basis points, against half the spread plus fees. Then compute how much faster you would need to be for the trade to be positive, and note that the answer is a latency figure rather than a research figure.
:::
:::
